stops.name: Meissen, the Elbe evening: Langethal and Middendorff found
stops.campa: First day's march, first halt: at Meissen, on a lovely spring evening, the corps' students gather by the Elbe over old Meissen wine, twenty strong at a long table, pledging friendship. A sergeant has already introduced Fröbel to a fellow Thuringian: Langethal; and here at the table Langethal presents his Berlin friend, the young divinity student Middendorff. Next morning the three visit the cathedral together. The lifelong brothers are found in the first bivouac of the war: Keilhau, Kindergarten, the whole gardened future, is seated at that table without knowing its own name.
stops.quote: Thus from the very first did we three join fast in a common struggle towards and on behalf of the higher life.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Havelberg, the armistice camp: Bauer closes the circle
stops.campa: Through the summer armistice the corps lies in quarters by the Havel, and camp-life does its quiet work: at Havelberg Fröbel strikes up with Bauer, the third friend of Langethal and Middendorff, and the narrow circle of his companions-in-arms is closed. Four students under arms, talking education between drills: the corps marches, skirmishes, endures the campaign into the Netherlands, and the friendship endures with it. He will say the war gave him no wounds and four brothers; the Fatherland he fought for turns out to be a schoolhouse not yet built.
stops.quote: It was more particularly at Havelberg, later on, that Bauer and I struck up a friendship together, which has ever since endured.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Berlin, the mineralogical museum: the godlike in the very small
stops.campa: The war done, Weiss calls his student back as assistant at the royal mineralogical museum. Alone in the locked, perfectly quiet room, ordering stones of the most minute dimensions, Fröbel receives the revelation of his middle life: even in these torn fragments of rock lie germs of developing energy; under all modifications, one law of development. The crystals become a mirror in which he descries mankind. Sweden offers him a professorship of mineralogy; he refuses it. A man to whom stones preach children cannot spend his life cataloguing stones.
stops.quote: I saw clearly, as never yet I had seen before, that the godlike is not alone in the great; for the godlike is also in the very small... And thereafter my rocks and crystals served me as a mirror wherein I might descry mankind, and man's development and history.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Griesheim an der Ilm, the Universal German Educational Institute
stops.campa: He resigns the museum, refuses the Stockholm chair, and walks out of Berlin with almost nothing, telling no one his aim. In the village of Griesheim on the Ilm, where his dead brother Christoph was minister, the widow gives him Christoph's three orphaned sons; his brother in Osterode sends two more. With five nephews in a village room, on 16 November 1816, Fröbel opens the Universal German Educational Institute: the whole reform of German education begun as one uncle keeping school for his brothers' children. He writes to Middendorff at Berlin: come, and bring Langethal.
stops.quote: I reckon, therefore, the duration of my present educational work from November 16th, 1816.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Keilhau, the move to the hillside
stops.campa: Middendorff has come in April, straight from Berlin, the first brother to answer; in June 1817 the little school moves to Keilhau, a hamlet folded into the hills by Rudolstadt, and takes root for good. Langethal arrives in September; a frame schoolhouse rises by November on ground Fröbel does not yet own. Poverty is the daily bread, but on this hillside the war-brothers convert their bivouac covenant into an educating household: gardens, wanderings, work, German dress, the child unfolded like the plant. Keilhau becomes the mother-house of everything that follows.
stops.quote: In June of the same year (1817) family reasons caused me to move from Griesheim to this place, Keilhau.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Berlin, marriage to Wilhelmine Hoffmeister
stops.campa: On 11 September 1818, in Berlin, Fröbel marries Henriette Wilhelmine Hoffmeister, a war-councillor's daughter of cultivated mind who has heard the idea in the man and chooses it with open eyes. She leaves the capital for a debt-ridden hamlet in the Thuringian hills, brings her fortune to the hungry institute, and becomes the first mother of the motherless man's great household. For twenty-one years she will carry Keilhau, Switzerland and Blankenburg beside him. The community calls the marriage what it is: the institute's own hearth being lit.

stops.name: Keilhau, growth, suspicion, and the inspector's verdict
stops.campa: The institute swells to some sixty pupils; the boys wear open collars and long hair, climb, garden, wander, and are educated by life itself, and reaction smells sedition in it. In the demagogue-hunting years Keilhau is denounced as a nest of revolution, and Prussia sends the inspector Zeh to examine it. He finds no conspiracy: he finds a wonderfully united family of sixty, living education instead of enduring it, and says so in his report. The verdict acquits, yet frightened parents withdraw their sons; the institute survives on faith and debt, as it always has.

stops.name: Keilhau, 'Die Menschenerziehung': the book of the eternal law
stops.campa: In 1826, out of the hillside's daily practice, Fröbel publishes The Education of Man, and opens it with a sentence that is the whole doctrine in miniature: an eternal law lives and works in all things. Education is named as leading man to a free representation of that inner law: not pouring in, but unfolding; the gardener's book written by the crystallographer. The weekly journal of the community carries on its masthead the six words that will one day stand on his gravestone: Come, let us live for our children.
stops.quote: In all things there lives and works an eternal law... This all-controlling law is necessarily based on an all-pervading, energetic, living, self-conscious, and hence eternal Unity... This Unity is God.
stops.quote_source: Die Menschenerziehung / The Education of Man (1826), tr. W. N. Hailmann, opening

stops.name: Helba, the national plan that heaven deferred
stops.campa: The Duke of Meiningen, won by the long autobiographical letter Fröbel has addressed to him, offers the estate of Helba for a great public educational institution: the Keilhau idea raised to the scale of a nation, with workshops, gardens and school as one organism. Plans are drawn, hopes rise high; then court intrigue and cautious counsellors strangle the scheme in the cradle by 1829. Fröbel walks away from the wreck carrying the plan's deepest layer intact: the conviction that the reform must begin further down, below the school, in earliest childhood.

stops.name: Schloss Wartensee, the castle on Lake Sempach
stops.campa: Invited by the composer Xavier Schnyder von Wartensee, Fröbel crosses into Switzerland in 1831 and opens an institute in the little castle above Lake Sempach. The liberal cantons hunger for the new education; the clergy of Lucerne scent heresy in the Protestant German and preach against him from the parishes. The school in the castle stays small under the pressure, but the seed shows its vigour: the townsmen of Willisau, having seen the work, petition to have it, priests notwithstanding. Exile, as always with Fröbel, is expansion wearing the mask of defeat.

stops.name: Willisau, the school in the teeth of the priests
stops.campa: At Willisau the townspeople give the Keilhau men a public institute, and it flourishes against a rising wall of clerical fury: sermons against the German educators, threats, the school made a battlefield of the cantonal war between old faith and new light. A public examination is held; the parents see their children and are won; enrollment climbs even as the pulpits thunder. Fröbel, twice denounced now, as demagogue in Prussia, as heretic in Lucerne, learns to read persecution as the shadow every real light casts.

stops.name: Burgdorf, the orphanage: Pestalozzi's own ground
stops.campa: The government of Bern calls Fröbel to direct the cantonal orphanage at Burgdorf: the very town where Pestalozzi began. The circle closes: the disciple keeps school on the master's first ground. Charged also with refresher courses for the canton's teachers, he watches the youngest orphans and the village children and the conviction ripens to certainty: all schooling comes too late; the decisive education happens before the sixth year, in play, at the mother's knee. In the orphan-house of Burgdorf, he who was half an orphan, the kindergarten becomes inevitable.
